Length
length
n. (extent from end to end; duration; rendering Hebrew orek, Greek mekos)
From the Saxon lengthu, from lang, long. Hebrew orek serves for both spatial extent and duration, so that length of days is as natural a phrase in that tongue as the length of a board.

Biblical Definition

Length in Scripture measures two things: space and life. Spatially it belongs to the tabernacle, the temple, and the city, where God gives exact dimensions and expects them kept — a fact that dignifies measurement itself and rebukes the notion that precision is unspiritual. Paul takes the vocabulary of measurement and applies it where it cannot finally be applied, praying that the saints “may be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height” (Ephesians 3:18) of the love of Christ — and then in the next breath calls that love a thing which passeth knowledge. The four dimensions are named precisely so that the reader will run out of them. Of life, length of days is a covenant blessing: Proverbs promises that wisdom brings “length of days, and long life, and peace” (Proverbs 3:2), and Moses tells Israel that the LORD “is thy life, and the length of thy days” (Deuteronomy 30:20) — the length is not an independent quantity but a Person's gift, and cleaving to him is the whole of the matter. The Psalter carries it past the grave: the king “asked life of thee, and thou gavest it him, even length of days for ever and ever” (Psalm 21:4), where the measure that began in a promise of long years on the land ends in the endless life of the Messiah and of those in him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Extent from end to end; also duration. Scripture measures buildings exactly, measures life as a covenant gift, and names the four dimensions of Christ's love in order to show they will not contain it.

expand to see more

LENGTH, n. [Sax. lengthu, from lang, long.] The extent of any thing material from end to end; the longest line which can be drawn through a body.

2. Extent of duration; as, the length of time, the length of a discourse.

3. Reach or expansion; extent; as, to run to a great length in argument.

4. Long continuance; as, the length of a disease.

5. At length, at full extent; also, at last, after a long time.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 3:18 — "May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height;"

Deuteronomy 30:20 — "That thou mayest love the LORD thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life, and the length of thy days: that thou mayest dwell in the land which the LORD sware unto thy fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them."

Proverbs 3:2 — "For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to thee."

Psalm 21:4 — "He asked life of thee, and thou gavest it him, even length of days for ever and ever."

Modern Corruption

Long life is treated as a bare medical achievement and the promise of length of days as an outdated bargain, while Ephesians 3:18 is read as though the love of Christ could be measured after all.

expand to see more

Where lifespan is regarded as a purely technical matter, the covenant framing of Deuteronomy 30:20 sounds primitive — as though obedience were a health regimen. But Moses is not offering a mechanism; he is naming a Person. He is thy life, and the length of thy days puts the years themselves in God's hand and makes cleaving to him the point rather than the price. The promise attached to the fifth commandment works the same way, and Paul repeats it to Christian children without embarrassment (Ephesians 6:2-3). Meanwhile the opposite error appears in devotional use of Ephesians 3:18, where the breadth and length and depth and height are treated as a set of measurements the diligent believer might eventually complete. Paul's own qualifier forbids it: the love he measures passeth knowledge. He piles up dimensions to exhaust them.

The principle to recover is that Scripture measures what God has measured and stops where he stops. The tabernacle has cubits because God gave cubits; the years of a life have a number because God numbers them; the love of Christ has four dimensions named and no total given. To insist on a number where God gave none is as much a failure of reverence as to despise the numbers he did give.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew orek covers extent and duration alike, so length of days is the natural idiom for long life. Greek mekos is spatial length; makrothumia, long-suffering, is length applied to patience.

expand to see more

Hebrew orek (H753) — length, of space or of days; from arak, to be long.

Hebrew arak (H748) — to prolong, to lengthen; that thy days may be long upon the land.

Greek mekos (G3372) — length; the dimension named in Ephesians 3:18 and Revelation 21:16.

Greek makros (G3117) — long, distant; of time and of space.

Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, length of temper; patience measured as duration.

Usage

"Of the dimensions of Christ's love: the breadth, and length, and depth, and height (Ephesians 3:18)."

"Of long life as covenant gift: he is thy life, and the length of thy days (Deuteronomy 30:20)."

"Of life prolonged for ever: thou gavest it him, even length of days for ever and ever (Psalm 21:4)."
